summary: In Greek mythology, Nephele (Ancient Greek: Νεφέλη, "cloud") is the cloud-nymph wife of Athamas of Boeotia and mother of Phrixus and Helle. When their stepmother Ino's plot doomed Phrixus to sacrifice, Nephele rescued the twins on a golden-fleeced ram — the fleece that later drew Jason to Colchis. Latin authors call her Nebula. A separate same-named cloud figure, the eidolon Zeus shaped like Hera for Ixion, is treated elsewhere in the atlas as Nubes.
etymology: Ancient Greek Nephélē (Νεφέλη), "cloud, mass of clouds." Latin Nebula.
cultCenters: Halos (Thessaly; alternate starting point of the flight)

sections.heading: Wife of Athamas
paragraphs: Nephele marries Athamas, Aeolid king in Boeotia (or Thessaly), and bears Phrixus and Helle. Athamas later takes Ino, Cadmus's daughter, who hates the twins. Ino roasts the seed-corn so crops fail, then bribes oracle-messengers to report that the dearth requires Phrixus's sacrifice (sometimes Helle's as well).

Before the killing, Nephele snatches up both children and sets them on a flying golden ram — a gift from Hermes in many tellings — bound for Colchis and King Aeëtes. Over the strait between Europe and Asia, Helle falls and drowns; the water is thereafter the Hellespont, "sea of Helle." Phrixus alone reaches Colchis, sacrifices the ram, and gives Aeëtes the Golden Fleece.

sections.heading: Homonym: the Ixion cloud
paragraphs: Ancient authors also use Nephele for the cloud-image of Hera that Zeus formed to expose Ixion's lust. Ixion assaults the eidolon, is bound to a fiery wheel, and the cloud bears Centaurus, ancestor of the centaurs. That figure is a distinct mythic persona from Athamas's wife; the atlas keeps the Ixion cloud under the id nubes-ixion.
